utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Good afternoon to everybody in and around the courtroom. Mr. Registrar, will you please call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you, and good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-04-81-T, The Prosecutor versus Momcilo Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Could we have appearances today, please, starting with the prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Good afternoon. It's Mark Harmon, Lorna Bolton, and Carmela Javier for the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. And for the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good afternoon. Daniela Tasic, Chad Mair, Kay Marshall, Colleen Rohan, Tina Drolec, Milos Androvic, Novak Lukic, and Gregor Guy-Smith on behalf of Mr. Perisic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much, Mr. Guy-Smith. Good afternoon -- or good morning out there in New York. How are you, Mr. Sacirbey, and everybody else? Can you hear me? They obviously don't hear us. Yeah, I'm speaking to you, but it looks like you don't hear us.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I also don't have any sound through my headphones, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bolton. Yes, there is obviously a problem. We're not connected yet.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, I'm not sure if you can you hear us, but we are not receiving any audio from your end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I can hear you, but can you hear me? You can't hear us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're not getting any audio. Are you hearing me now. Sorry, can you hear me? Hello? I can hear you very well. Can't you hear me. Thank you so much. Okay. Fine. Good. Just for the record I just want to say that once again today we're still sitting pursuant to Rule 15 bis as Judge Picard is still held up in another trial, Stanisic and Simatovic. I wanted to say to you, Mr. Sacirbey, that once again, we go through the ritual to say that you are still bound by the declaration you made at the beginning of your testimony to tell the truth, the whole truth and nothing else but the truth. Is that okay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I understand. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. We ended yesterday's proceedings looking at a particular document which was 1D00-1843, page 26, which was a quote of Lord Owen, and I ask that that be admitted into evidence, that particular page.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I don't know what the relevance is. I thought my friend was going to develop this issue. I'm not sure what the relevance is of a quote from Lord Owen to any material issue at this proceeding.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, we can start that way -- that's fine. Let's start the day that way and go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm not sure I understand what you are saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I choose not to respond to Madam Bolton's remarks at this time. So I leave it in the Court's fine hands right now. If the Court is willing to admit the document, fine. Otherwise, we'll proceed and go from there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The Court does what the parties ask them to do, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is my request at this time that the document -- that page be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I have no recollection of what the document was all about. Can we see the document again, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It's page 26, Your Honour, and the quote is: "Nothing is simple in the Balkans. History pervades everything and complexities confound even the most careful study. Never before in over 30 years of public life have I had to operate in such" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Please slow down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please, slow down. And you just want that page.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yep.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It's admitted. May it please be given an exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, as Exhibit D127.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't have Mr. Sacirbey. There we go.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I would like to start today discussing with you the matter of your intelligence or information sources while you were the ambassador at the United Nations. As I understand your testimony thus far, you obtained information from international media sources; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You obtained information from some of your colleagues at the United Nations, and by colleagues I mean both ambassadors as well as members of staff who were working at the United Nations during the period of time that you were there; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You also obtained information from what I will call for the moment the ground, and by that I mean such individuals as your president, President Izetbegovic. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Would it be fair to say that you also received information from other sources on the ground, such as Sefer Halilovic, Rasim Delic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, if you mean by Bosnian military. On a few occasions, I don't remember that I discussed this with Sefer Halilovic but at least on a few occasions I discussed it with General Rasim Delic, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And did have you conversations with Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not even meet Naser Oric until after the war and only on one occasion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you have -- and I appreciate that you did not meet him, which I take it means that you did not have a face-to-face conversation with him. Did you have any telephone or other forms of communication with him, such as satellite phone or telex?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I would recall any direct conversation with him, nor -- at least no one that represented himself as Naser Oric.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And did you have any contact with Enver Hadzihasanovic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Frankly, doesn't even sound familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If I were to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may have been --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I may be pronouncing his name incorrectly. I may be pronouncing his name incorrectly, but if I were to say to you, It's my understanding that he was the chief of the Supreme Command Staff of the BiH army in November of 1993, would that be of any assistance to you, with regard to, first of all, such a name?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. Well, first of all, I just don't recall having a conversation with him. The one -- the one name that may escape me is the commander of the Cerska enclave, who, on several occasions, did call the mission of BiH in the spring of 1993. And that's the one that I'm conscious of not skipping somehow.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you that the one name that may escape you is that commander, when he called you how did you speak with him? Did you speak with him on a satellite phone?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe it was a satellite phone, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or might have been some other connection out of the enclave, but we in fact received it on a regular telephone.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever have any conversations concerning what was going on, going on, on the ground with General Talijan, this is spelled T-a-l-i-j-a-n, who was located in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person that I had the greatest communication from the military was actually General Jovan Divjak because he visited New York in the fall of 1992 for the General Assembly session and we spent a lot of time together, and after that, it was much more sporadic in terms of my communication with any military staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, just so that we expedite matters, can I suggest you listen to the question and try to be precise in your answer. The question was: Did you ever have conversations with General Talijan. We'll deal with Divjak --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: And the answer is I don't -- I don't believe I've had conversations with General Talijan, at least not that I recall.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to other members of who I believe were in the 1st Corps of the BiH army in Sarajevo, did you have conversations with either Vahid Karavelic or Nedzad Ajnadzic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly, but I just don't recall any such conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We seem to have having a failure of video here. Mr. Sacirbey's face is frozen in time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. But can we hear him when he speaks?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes, I can hear him, but I can't see his facial expressions.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We can see you and hear you perfectly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, expect that your video that side is frozen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can go through this limited part of the examination in this -- in this sense, because it is going to be basically dealing with the same subject matter. But there will come a time when I really do need to be able to see the gentleman's facial expressions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let's hope in the meantime that it gets sorted out.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. I take it that's a compatible way of working with the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, now it's gone from bad to worse.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honours, can you hear us and see us?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Indeed, I can hear you now. And can you hear us?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] We can hear you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes we can, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Sacirbey. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I think we have attended to the audio issue, but not to the video issue. But I will proceed as I said I would with this particular -- when I finish this area, then we will have to deal with the video issue, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I left off asking you some names. I'm going to continue in that regard. Did you have conversation with General Hazim Sadic who I believe was in the 2nd Corps in Tuzla, also a member of the BiH army?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not that I recall, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mehmet Alagic who was in Zenica, 3rd Corps.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did have conversations with him, but I think that was only toward the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Toward the end of the war would that have -- can you be any more specific in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I certainly remember meeting him in 1995. I may have met him as early as 1994. I'm just not precise on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to this particular gentleman, do you recall or do you have a memory of when he was the commander of Zenica, for what period of time?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I -- I believe he was commander for -- if not the entire conflict, certainly the back end of it when I meant him. I don't remember the date that he was pointed. I believe was commander through the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by "through the conflict" do you mean until the signing of the Dayton Accord?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I were to tell you have I information that he was commander in Zenica until the 26th of February, 1994, would be have any reason to argue with me in that regard?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't. I do know that I met him in a role as a military commander and for whatever reason my memory of him may be in the connection of other roles that he played in the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you met him, did you meet him stateside, or did you meet him on the ground in Bosnia-Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was in Bosnia and Herzegovina. If I'm not mistaken, it was also outside of Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever have a conversation with Dzemal Merdan?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, I did not hear the name, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Dzemal Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Zeman, I think, is the pronunciation of the first name. And, again, I may have had conversations with him toward the end of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Just stopping here for a moment. With regard to the gentlemen who were in the military you had conversations with, are those conversations that you noted? And by "noted" I mean memorialized in some fashion to be used for whatever purposes you deemed necessary in front of the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. By and large if I in fact used information in the context of the United Nations and therefore in the context of these proceedings, I would have to limit that to only three or four individuals. And that -- again, I emphasise that General Jovan Divjak, General Rasim Delic, I emphasise the commander of Cerska; and I think those would be the three main military commanders that I would have dealt with. My staff may have dealt with others, and I'm quite certain that they did and may have in fact obtained the information. But I don't recall in the context that which are you now describing that I dealt with any more than three or four individuals from the military.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to mention one other name to you that I want to know whether you dealt with personally. And then after that I'm going to mention a series of names to you to see if these are names that your staff ever reported to you with regard to having conversations about what was going on, on the ground. The name that I'm going mention to you with regard to you have personal conversations with would be Arif Pasalic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I know the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Is that a gentleman that you spoke to during the war concerning what was going on, on the ground?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If it was, it might have only in a casual conversation, not something that I would relayed in the connection of my responsibilities.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say "in a casual conversation," I take it that would have been a casual conversation in Bosnia and not in New York?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. The names I'm now going to mention to you because I think you've told us that you only met with three or four people - and if any of the names do ring a bell do let me know - are names that would have been reported to, potentially by your staff. Mustafa Isovic from the 4th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Don't -- don't recall anything specific about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Atif Dudakovic from the 5th Corps?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Definitely someone that I know, met on several occasions once the Bihac area was liberated. The communications during the war, I -- I believe he managed to get some communications to our mission. I don't remember speaking to him actually during the majority of the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: General Galib Hodzic.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know the name, but nothing specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: From the 6th Crops. From the 7th Corps, Commander General Mehmet Alagic, I think you've mentioned. Did you ever deal with a gentleman whose name -- who was the Chief of Staff of the 7th Corps, Fikret Cusic or Cuskic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing specific that I would recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Did you ever have any dealings with a gentleman by the name of Fikret Abdic?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do know who the gentleman is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Tell the Chamber who Fikret Abdic was.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Fikret Abdic at the time of my involvement with Bosnia and Herzegovina was the leader of something -- the so-called Krajina area of Bosnia and Herzegovina, and it was a separatist group under the leadership of Mr. Fikret Abdic. As I understand he is serving prison now in Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say he was a leader of a separatist group, a separatist Group from where? From -- from the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, from Croatia, from Slovenia, Slovakia? Where was he a leader of a separatist group from?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Primarily Bosnia and Herzegovina, although they occupied also a piece of the territory of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when did this separatist group initially form itself?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Somewhere right around the outset of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And by right around the outset of the war, are you talking about before or after Izetbegovic was elected president?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, President Izetbegovic was elected president well before the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Or he was elected a member of the Presidency and, of course, the Chair of that Presidency ultimately.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Am I correct in my understanding that, as a matter of fact, there came a time when this individual, Fikret Abdic, ran against President Izetbegovic before he was elected as president?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They certainly were, if you would, concurrence. I'm not sure it would be appropriate to say they ran against each other, because we were talking about a collective Presidency of Bosnia-Herzegovina. But they certainly had a different vision.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you said they certainly had a different vision, you're referring to a different vision from that which was held by President Izetbegovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm saying they did not agree.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And others obviously.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: They did not agree with each other on the future of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And, to your knowledge, was this gentleman, Fikret Abdic, was he a Muslim?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know if he was practicing or not. But at least by his Ethnic identity, he would have been considered Bosniak.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to the issue of whether he was practicing or not, was, to your knowledge, this particular separatist leader supported by any other countries?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We believe he was supported by Serbia and Montenegro.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. And when would that have been? Would that have been throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would -- that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: At this time, I am done with my list of names and need to be in a position where I can have some face recognition.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Mr. Registrar, can you try and get us -- apparently we have to disconnect to be able to get the video.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Can you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yeah, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry about that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... I can hear you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apart from the names that we've just mentioned, I take it that it would be fair to say that you also received information from various members of your government back in Bosnia; correct? And once again when I say information --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When I say information, I'm referring to information that you ultimately made a determination would be utilized in your capacity as the representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whether I was always in a position to always make that determination, of course, was dependant on whether the information to me for my consideration, or whether I was instructed to actually provide it to the United Nations Security Council Secretary-General Assembly by my government. I did not necessarily always have that discretion.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your answer. With regard to information that was flowing back and forth between you and your government, you were concerned that there were leaks in your government, and specifically in your foreign ministry, were you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Always was, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And in that regard, part of your concern was that individuals in your government would be leaking information to those entities that you perceived as your enemy. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly Belgrade, where some officials might have had past relationships; that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say where some officials might have had past relationships, are you referring to those individuals in your government who were identified as being ethnically Serb?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually more likely than not, I would have been concerned about Bosniaks more than Serbs. I -- I certainly did not identify leaks or threats on the basis of ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With regard to those individuals who you were concerned about leaking information, can you identify for the Chamber who those individuals were?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that be would highly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton. Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Again, I just have a relevance issue with respect to this line of questioning. This wasn't a matter that came up in Examination-in-chief, so pursuant to our guidelines, it would have to have some relevance to either credibility of this witness or to my friend's case. And if it does have that relevance, it's just not apparent to me at this point, and I'm referring specifically to guideline 8.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Bolton. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me double-check to make sure which guideline Ms. Bolton is referring to, and then I will respond. A central issue in this case is that of notice. Notice is obtained by the passage of information. We have heard much testimony about various methods and manners by which, potentially, information could be made aware to the public at large and our to client in specific. With regard to the -- with regard to the particular issue of leaks, especially when viewing it in the context of a conflict, and more particularly in the context of a conflict that involves, among other things, both internal and external military decisions, the issue of leaks, one would think, would be something which is of import and germane to the analysis that we're undergoing. With regard to the question of those leaks, since this was a matter of some concern for Mr. Sacirbey, identifying those individuals who he was concerned with could well lead us to, and I say this most specifically, that I am not on a fishing expedition, could well lead us to intercepts that either substantiate or reject such a position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, my problem with your line of questioning is that you are just asking the witness who he had contact with, and you don't telling us what it is he discussed with these people. So We don't see the relevance. And when you talk of leaks, I don't even know what is suppose to have been leaked. Secrets, of course, intelligence, confidential information. What information which would go to notice or -- which is what you say is the issue here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me proceed with your -- with your concern. With regard to those individuals who we initially discussed who were all of the military ilk, Did you have discussions with them concerning the military situation on the ground during the period of conflict?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to those conversations, in a general sense, you discussed with them such things as their fighting ability; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I believe that would be an accurate characterization.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to their fighting ability, you discussed with them such issues as the availability of munitions, weapons, and --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And other instruments of war. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Particularly anti-tank weapons, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You discussed with them the shipments that were going to be made to them; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think now you're asking me either a general or specific question. If you're suggesting, did I discuss with them specific shipments? Or am I -- are you talking about general shipments?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I will first talk with about you about general shipments and then we'll talk about the specific in a bit.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay. In general we certainly discuss what was available to them. Certainly my personal knowledge as to the arrival of any specific shipments, I think at this point on, I will have to consult with my counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it that with regard to that particular issue, it is your opinion that any answers would you give in that regard would tend to incriminate you. Is that what you're asserting now?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is my opinion -- absolutely not. I think it's only wise for me to discuss this matter with my counsel. That's all that I'm saying.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm going to ask on a ruling on that from the Court because I don't believe that is the reason why he was counsel present. This is a direct inference in the fact-finding process, and there has been no legally recognizable assertion made that would allow for such a unique circumstance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's my respectful submission, up until this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It may be that the witness doesn't know what kinds of shipments my friend is talking about, and there may be some confusion as between counsel and the witness. We don't know what materials he is talking about, and so I think until that is clarified, the witness is perhaps on a different page than Defence counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: My only problem is that, here, we haven't really heard from the witness why he wanted to have counsel with him. He has asked to have counsel with him. He has asked to have counsel with him, and we've said counsel must be with him. He now asking to consult his counsel. We have surmised why he needs counsel to be with him, and the summation that we made is precisely the proposition you put to him whether he is going to incriminate himself by answering the question or not. And he says, no, that's not the issue. But we don't know why he called counsel. So ... but we have allowed him to have counsel, and if we have allowed him to have counsel, I think he must consult counsel when he feels the need to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With all due respect, Your Honour, the purpose of counsel in this regard, as I understood the Court's ruling, was to deal with the limited issue of whether or not questions propounded to him could potentially place him in a position, the response to which would lead to incrimination. And on those grounds, he was afforded the right to counsel. Which, as I said some time ago, something that I fully support. The fact that he has got a lawyer sitting in the room does not in and of itself allow him to confer with that lawyer, if the conversation with that lawyer is outside of the specific legal purpose for which he asked for the lawyer in the first place. Now we're having a deviation from the very reason why this whole matter began. And if you recall the matter, began with a motion from the Prosecution, with regard to the limits of cross-examination on the very specific issue of self-incrimination. Not any other issue. At this point in time, to have the witness be allowed to confer with counsel on anything outside of the specific purpose for which he asked for counsel initially, it is our respectful submission, it would be outside of the intent and order of this Chamber. In addition, there's another potential legal matter that needs to be addressed, which is something that Your Honour raised early on, which is that his counsel - and if I mispronounce your name, sir, I do apologise, Mr. Guirguis, did not have standing. And you made a very specific ruling with regard to for what purpose he was present and what he could do as a lawyer on behalf of Mr. Sacirbey. The position taken now is dramatically distinct from where we began this particular legal analysis and legal journey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I provide some insight into this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: No, sir, you have asked for leave to consult with your lawyer. The Court must resolve the matter before you can speak. Yeah, thank you very much. I mean --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might refer you, if it is of any assistance --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm assisted.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, could I just address that last point that my friend was raising.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: There is an issue in terms of the role Mr. Guirguis would play, in that initially my friend is correct, in that there was an indication he didn't have standing, but then last Friday, you will recall, we had an exchange where I was asking -- or sorry, a week ago Friday, asking about my raising objections in the area of the allegations from Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I understood from that exchange that, in respect of that narrow issue, that being the allegations, that it would be Mr. Guirguis who would have to respond or raise any objections, and not something that I would do. Do I -- does this ring you a bell, Your Honour? Have I misunderstood again your ruling?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. I remember. But it is for -- I'm sorry, sir, can you spell this name for me. I hate mispronouncing people's names. What is counsel's name again?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: It's Guirguis. G-u-i-r-g-u-i-s.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it's pronounced?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: He is he laughing at me, so --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Guirguis, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Guirguis, okay. Now, yes, the way I understand -- and I said I'm indebted to Mr. Guy-Smith for reminding us the reason for his presence. The way I understand Mr. Guirguis' presence is that when an issue does arise which would prejudice Mr. Sacirbey for purposes for which Mr. Guirguis is present, he would then say to him, Sorry, you need to talk to me and -- before you answer that question. And he can do so either raising his hand or saying that, yes, he doesn't have standing. He doesn't have to address the Court, but he can give advice to his client.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. So to that extent, yes, I must defer to what you say, sir. You are may proceed. Objection overruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. My question was then ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: My question then is: With regard to your personal knowledge as to the arrival of any specific shipments, that's the place where we are now, and in that regard --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- did you -- did you discuss with the military on the ground, and specifically such individuals as General Delic, the arrival of specific shipments of munitions and arms and other instruments of war during the time that you were the ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina at the United Nations between 1992 and the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Guy-Smith, as you know the allegations that are directed at me may have been portrayed in some particular way in the media or even by yourself. But they actually --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, sir, I'm going to interrupt you now. This time I am going to interrupt you. I've asked you a specific question; I expect a specific answer. Thereafter, sir --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thereafter, sir, you may explain it. However, this is it not a bully poppet [phoen] for you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will invoke Rule 90(E).

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You're taking the position that this particular -- that the answer to this particular question will tend to incriminate you.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It may.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Proceeding --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me. In that regard, I think at this point in time, we need the benefit of the position that his counsel is going to take.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Rule 90(E) reads --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: The position is that this is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because what I'm going to ask is, pursuant to 90(E), I'm going to ask the Chamber to compel him to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. What the witness had alluded to in his response is a concern that the answer to this question may incriminate him, and he said - sorry, I wanted to find his exact words - basically, he's concerned not just here but again with the allegations in Bosnia and Herzegovina. So I would ask, then, in light of that response that we go into private -- I guess private session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I think before we do that, I don't think that that's necessarily what he is saying. He may well be saying that, and perhaps we need to get clarification on that, first of all. He may be asserting that is he going to be prosecuted somewhere else in the world for this answer. There is another issue that arises here, which is that if one views 90(E), there is a remedy, and the remedy is clear, which is contained in the third sentence of 90(E).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sir, the Chamber wants you to take this moment to consult with counsel before we break, and tell us what your position is. I know that you said you're invoking Rule 90(E). Do you need any further advice from your counsel on that, or are you happy to stand by what you have just said?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I would like to have the advice of my counsel further.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to confer with him before we take the break?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Please do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Kind of unusual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A bit unusual.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I don't know that it would be unusual that you consult in confidence with your counsel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Couldn't they mute us -- mute themselves, or mute us?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry. I was speaking. Solicitor/client privilege would be breached by the presence of The Registrar to hear their conversations, so in order to have Confidence, they have to take place just between the counsel and the Client.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This might be one area where it may be of some assistance coming from the same general tradition and jurisdiction. The chances are probably pretty good they're going to be spending some time discussing this matter with each other. And perhaps we could do at this time is have Madam Registrar peak her head out the door and go from there. But I leave it in your -- I leave it your capable hands, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The part -- she is not in court now. But my problem is that I thought this was a very simple matter. Do I stand by my 90(E)'s request or don't I? Yes or no, full stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... That's what I thought too, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't think it needed any further discussion and ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apparently --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because that is the only purpose for which counsel is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour's, I apologise. Should I invite counsel and the witness to come back in?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: It would be very helpful if you could, ma'am, because we're well into the break time now, and we want to take the break.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] I'm on my way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Just before we take the break, to say that -- yeah, the Chamber Was taken aback by the fact that you left the room. We'll take the break and come back at 4.00. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I guess, when we went out, when we went for break, you had just come back from conferring with counsel, Mr. Sacirbey. What's your position?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: May I ask my counsel to speak, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Actually, Mr. Sacirbey, we don't want arguments. We just want your position. Do you want to answer? You don't want to answer? That is really the question that I'm asking you. As I said, your counsel --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is -- I had understood that I standing to make these objections. I don't plan on a lengthy argument, but I do plan on establishing the basis for Mr. Sacirbey' objection and raising a Rule 90(E), which I understand was the Court's prior ruling.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes. The basis we understand. The basis is of you self-incrimination, and that's it, you know. And really what we want to know is what is Mr. Sacirbey saying, yes, he doesn't want to answer the question because he will self-incriminate, or no?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Well, I think Mr. Sacirbey would just take exception to the suggestion that it would necessarily incriminate him, instead, what he is saying is that there are issues which may be raised --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, what is he doing now is precisely [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... is precisely in violation of what you have asked.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Guirguis, we must stop you from talking. Mr. Sacirbey, do you want to answer the question, or you feel you cannot answer the -- you don't want to answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I feel that I cannot answer the question without the possibility of risk to my legal status.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. And your legal status, you mean self-incrimination? That's the reason your counsel is here.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, again, we have -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I beg your pardon. I was just saying I don't know whether the parties have any -- still have any submissions. I think we have heard the submissions of both parties, and unless there is something that they want to add, we can rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just like my objection - this is Peter Guirguis - my objection noted for the record that I have not been heard on this matter. But the Court may proceed, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guirguis, there will be no objection put on the record by you because have you no standing before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have submitted, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. The -- Mr. Sacirbey, your protection is granted. You don't have to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: For purposes of the record, considering that Rule 90(E) does have a provision that not only safeguards the witnesses concerns with regarding to the privilege against self-incrimination but also would allow for the explanation and examination of facts that are germane to the defence of General Perisic, we would interpose an objection. We would request that the testimony be compelled pursuant to order by this Chamber. And given the Chamber's concern or inclination that I'm inferring from the ruling just made that testimony, which is compelled in this fashion, shall not be used as evidence in a subsequent prosecution against Mr. Sacirbey for any offence other than false testimony which we would call perjury.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That protection protects Mr. Sacirbey within this Tribunal, obviously doesn't protect him against courts in the rest of the world. These are just no rules of procedure; they are not substantive law. And these are Rules of Procedure by the ICTY, not by the UN, so we don't bind anybody outside of this Tribunal. Secondly, the relevance of shipments of arms and ammunition to the question of notice to Mr. Perisic eludes me. So I'm not quite sure that this is relevant. So there are two grounds on which I do that. The Chamber does allow Mr. Sacirbey not to answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During the period of time that you were an ambassador for Bosnia and Herzegovina, you met with various officials or individuals from a variety of states for the purpose of obtaining weapons, did you not?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And in that regard, you specifically made arrangements to purchase ammunition and weapons from a number of individuals, including members of the Russian delegation. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I should invoke Rule 90(E), Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: To me this is the same topic that we have just ruled on, and I was surprised that in fact you didn't invoke this Rule 90(E) with respect to the very first question, after the ruling.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, we just -- I'm trying to be as forthcoming as possible, at the same time, obviously, protect my legal interests. So I hope you can appreciate my efforts at that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Granted. It's the same topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You also met with members of the Iranian delegation for the purpose --

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Could counsel, if this is the same topic, be instructed to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was just going to do that, Madam. Counsel, otherwise we are going to be sort of -- you are going to be putting questions, and I'm going to say -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... Very well, and for --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would like to you move on, please, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: During -- well, first of all, I understand what the Chamber's position is, and because the Chamber has asked me to move on, I will. I would note an objection. I believe that this goes directly to issues concerning credibility of this particular witness, and I want to make sure that the Chamber is aware of the fact of my concerns in this regard, but I will move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You, during your tenure as ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, continually pressed for the lifting of the embargo under United Nations Resolution 713. True?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You made that particular issue of concern not only with the United Nations but also with various members of the United States government, specifically Senator Dole; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: From Senator Dole to Richard Holbrooke; that is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: You had occasion to meet, if I'm not mistaken, by, I'm saying you, that would have been you, President Izetbegovic, and, I believe Dr. Slavic to meet in the basement of -- the basement area of the United Nations with Mr. Holbrooke concerning the embargo issue; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. I believe I'm on the record in that meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to Mr. Holbrooke, could you tell the Chamber who you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to, at that time, the undersecretary of the US State Department who was also directly responsible for the negotiations management of the, what was probably called internally, the Balkan crisis or the Bosnian-Herzegovina conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Holbrooke told to you cease and desist pressures on the American Congress with regard to the lifting of this embargo under United Nations Resolution 713, and you would be assured of supplies of arms coming from Iran; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to make the direct quote, which I have been cited for, Mr. Guy-Smith, which is, we could be allowed to receive weapons from any source we wanted to, including Iran. So Iran was not the exclusive potential source that Mr. Holbrooke outlined.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: In that regard, did you discuss with Mr. Holbrooke those other sources that you would be receiving potentially weapons from, apart from Iran?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Personally, I did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I could have a moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to your last response, you said, personally, you did not. Am I led to believe that there were discussions between Mr. Holbrooke and others concerning the transfer of weapons to Bosnia-Herzegovina in violation of Resolution 713 that occurred with other members of your government or military?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: There may have been -- Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, Mr. Sacirbey. Sorry, I take that the witness can't see me, so I have to speak quickly before he starts to answer, and I apologise, because I sometimes interrupt other speakers. Again, the issue of whether Bosnia-Herzegovina was obtaining weapons in terms of the issues before this trial, I'm not sure are relevant, certainly in the involvement of Mr. Holbrooke, again, I'm not understanding the relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, relevance?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thus far, we have learned from Mr. Sacirbey that information sources with regard to what various positions were concerning, at a minimum, the passage of United Nations Resolution 713, were not only mixed, in terms of the interpretation of that particular Resolution, but also that, apparently outside of the formality of the Security Council, outside of the formality of the General Assembly, there were deals that were being cut. The deals that were being cut are deals that directly go to the issue of what it was reasonable for any individual who was in possession of that information to understand about the state of affairs. The Prosecution has asserted, and I think rather loudly and strongly, that the passing of the variety of resolutions, in effect, establishes not only the legality of various positions but the duty that it would impose on others, and specifically the duty that it would impose on Mr. Perisic, if indeed you have, as we do here, indications that there were violations of these specific resolutions, the extent to which they can be taken at face value as having mandatory effect, as having legal effect, as having a binding effect, is certainly something which this Chamber will necessarily have to consider when making a determination of the impact of any of the publication of these -- of these materials to the parties in general. And if, ultimately, it determines that this is information that Mr. Perisic had specifically, the impact of that information to him as well. Under a totality of the circumstances test, it is reasonable to assert, and it is reasonable to consider whether or not where there have been violations of the self-same resolutions that are being used for purposes of establishing a basis of liability, culpability, obligation, or duty, that an individual possessed of such information could reasonably believe, objectively believe, that it was an alternative matter and have an alternative approach to those particular promulgations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, it's -- I will put it to you real simple. Judge, if I say to you, You can't go there, and if you do go there, you will get in trouble. And you see everybody going there and nobody getting in trouble, you may think that perhaps my statement to you is not an accurate one. And certainly not one which you would follow or rely upon in any respect whatsoever. And if you have, as we seem to have here, and I use the terminology quite specifically, a cynical world in which violations of the -- of the initial resolution, that theoretically is supposed to stop the conflict and conflagration is occurring, then it is certainly something to be taken under consideration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Let me say this. The person on trial here is Mr. Perisic and not Mr. Sacirbey, or is it any of the Bosnian army people. And to say that because somebody said you shall not steal, and other people are stealing and they are not caught and not prosecuted, therefore, you steal, which is what I understand you to be saying, which almost borders on a cousin of tu quoque.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And that doesn't sound to me like a defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Absolutely not. That's not what I'm saying, Your Honour. And I really don't want you to in any sense whatsoever think that is what is going on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The statement that somebody says, Don't go there, and you see other people going there and nothing happening to them, and you think you also can go there without consequences, to me, is something like saying, Well, there's a law that says we shall not steal, people do steal, people don't get prosecuted, I might as well steal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand -- I understand your concern. Before we go any further, I have been patient in holding back on this issue. There has been, as far as I can tell, at least two separate occasions in which there have been communications between Mr. Sacirbey's lawyer and himself through writing, which is not permitted. We have a tape here, so if there is any question about it, it can be reviewed. But I would admonish Mr. Guirguis to stay in his position as a lawyer for the purpose of dealing with the issue of self-incrimination and not engage in counselling Mr. Sacirbey with regard do his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I didn't observe that. And if, indeed, you did do that, Mr. Guirguis, you are so warned. You do not have to engage in communication with Mr. Sacirbey unless you want to -- you want to advise him, and in which case, you shall do so through the Court, or he shall do so through the Court, that he would like to take advice form you on a specific issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KEHOE
utterances.text: I think --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: So to be clear, Your Honour, so that -- if I may, Mr. Guy-Smith. Your Honour, so I can clearly understand the Court' ruling because it is not my intent in any way to violate the Court throughout this. If it is my intent to direct the witness not to answer a question or to invoke Rule 90(E), how would you like me to communicate that to the witness? Would you like me to interrupt the questioning and interrupt the Court and inform him formally in front of the Court? Or may I do so privately as between us? Which is what I had understood the ruling before to be and what I -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I expressed my surprise that you left the courtroom and went to confer outside. It is a very simple counselling that he needs on that issue. Yes, you may answer the question; yes, you may not answer the question. You don't really need to leave the court for that to do it privately. If you must indicate, maybe you might do so by raising your hand, and we will stop, and we'll ask Mr. Sacirbey to hear what you have to say. And you can tell Mr. Sacirbey, and Mr. Sacirbey can tell us.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: What I'm getting at this, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Because I think that going towards the notion of tu quoque is not only ill-advised, it is incorrect in terms of what I'm saying to you. Under the principle of in dubio pro reo and under the jurisprudence of this Tribunal, if there is an objectively reasonable alternative explanation for why an individual acted in a particular fashion or if there is an objectively reasonable alternative explanation which is distinct from that of guilt, the Trial Chamber must of necessity adopt that interpretation. Now here what we're dealing is the issue of perception. And the issue of perception is going to be rather critical to you at the conclusion of this case, with regard to what the motivations were of General Perisic. If you take -- it seems as if Judge David wishes to say something, so I will stop.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Can you finish, Mr. Guy-Smith. If you could be brief, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This gentleman's testimony has been replete with identifying resolutions which, as the Chamber knows, I objected to him reading from the resolutions and interpreting them, because they were documents, that I took in that position, stood for themselves, and the Court could read them as well as anyone else. Mr. Sacirbey has put a spin on these documents. It is his spin, and I don't think it's necessarily something which he can be faulted for because of his particular position with regard to not only the conflict but his position as a diplomat and his position in regards to this case. But that does not discount the importance of this Court being aware of the fact that the mice were scurrying about throughout this conflict and all of that information and all of the things that were occurring potentially affected the perception, the thinking, and ultimately the actions of General Perisic. And to deny an inquiry into this particular area is to begin the process of cutting off an aspect of what, in our respectful submission, is an appropriate line of inquiry and is an appropriate line of consideration for the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you saying Mr. Perisic was aware of what was happening, what was -- what the Bosnian army was doing and what Mr. Sacirbey was doing, and therefore he went and did what he did because he saw them doing what they were doing?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, indeed not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Then I don't see the relevance.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I don't think that I would need to have to say that in order for this to become part of your consideration. I really -- I don't think that's where the inquiry should be at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Are you done with your argument? Are you done with your response?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you so much. Do you have response, ma'am? You made an objection.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I stand by the objection. I still don't think the relevance has been established, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Objection upheld.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Could I have 1D03-1477 up on the screen.

utterances.text: [Via videolink] Could counsel please identify the tab number.

utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.text: That's a different number.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm afraid that's unreleased, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I seem to be saying the wrong thing. 1D03-1477.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay, can you see that -- do you have the title page on your screen -- do you have the title page available to you?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

"A. Yes. And in fact its primary right to defend itself was the one that legally dominated." And my question to you, sir, is: Is one of the member states that you're referring to when you made that statement yesterday, the United States of America?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that's a largely accurate statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could now have in the same document, the last four numbers would be 1631. And if we could move -- you need to move down, yes. And it would be the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH

utterances.text: I think, Madam Bolton, the question was: When you talked about violation of air space, did you refer to this? The answer is, yes, I did; no, I didn't. utterances.text: I think I actually heard the question reformulated, to some extent, by His Honour. So it may be -- if you can restate it for me, I want it make sure I'm precise here to your question, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.text: With regard to the sentence that I have read out loud, which you have had the opportunity to read, were you aware of there being a violation of air space on February 10th, 12th, 17th, and the 23rd of 1995 as described in this particular paragraph?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Beyond the report that you have read to me, and beyond the request that I made of the US government at that time for humanitarian airdrops, I'm not aware of anything of that sort.

utterances.text: I'm trying to make this shorter, not longer, so if I could have a second.

utterances.text: Going to 1675. The 1675, I'm sorry -- thank you. Down to the very -- down to the bottom.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the last paragraph, it is -- which says: "Izetbegovic and the radicalization of the Muslim political leadership, it is the abandonment of secular and democratic principles by the Bosnian Muslim political leadership, particularly by President Izetbegovic" --

utterances.text: [Via videolink] Your Honour, can that paragraph be zoomed in a bit more. I apologise.

Under the leadership of President Izetbegovic, the Muslims have in the years since the dissolution of Yugoslavia, frequently tried to calm the fears and suspicions of the Serb and Croat minorities by emphasizing a commitment to secularism, and the protection of minority democratic rights. With regard to the views expressed there, sir, were those views the kind of views that you were talking about, that were expressed during your tenure as an ambassador to Bosnia-Herzegovina for the United Nations?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I think that document -- I think that document both came out and refers to a period after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. What I'm getting at is the -- the underlying concern that is contained therein. utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, again, emphasizing that this document refers to a period after the war, it is my view, also, that in fact the Dayton Accords did in many ways betray secularism and did in fact create a new feudal system within Bosnia and Herzegovina. It is it my view that not only Dayton agreement but, in fact, in many ways it has been implemented since the conclusion of the war has promoted, what I call a European apartheid, where people are encouraged to live in ethnic ghettos, rather than promoting a true notion of a pluralistic multi-ethnic Bosnia. utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Just before you continue, Madam Stenographer, Mr. Lukic has been so quite right through this proceedings, if you could please delete his name from the record. Thank you so much. Just protecting you, Mr. Lukic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Finally -- well, not finally, I apologise. If we could now go to last four numbers 2079, which would be page 603. utterances.text: Not specifically, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.text: You had earlier discussed with us that some of the information that you obtained, and I'm not sure whether you obtained that information firsthand or second-hand, but that some of the information that you had obtained had been obtained from CIA intelligence sources; correct?

utterances.text: I have never received a direct briefing that I am at least aware of from someone who identified himself as a CIA operative.

utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I had extensive discussions with people who may have had either CIA connections, or may have been CIA, for all I know. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And what I'm asking you, because I think have you established for us that you have no contemporaneous records of such conversations, as you sit here today, information that you were led to believe came from the CIA was information upon which you relied; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Again, to the extent -- again to the extent that I was confident that it was accurate, and, of course, depends on what purpose would I rely for it.

utterances.text: Okay. Looking at this particular document, in 1994, there are a series of dates, those being January 22nd, February 7th, March 16th, April 4th, April 27th.

utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you have any reason to disbelieve that the information that is contained in this particular chart which is information from the CIA concerning actual or proposed arms shipments is inaccurate, incorrect, or in any other fashion --

utterances.text: I have in reason --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- unreliable?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no particular reason to believe -- I have no particular reason to believe that it is an inaccurate. Also, on the contrary, I have no reason to believe it's necessarily accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I see. With regard to your answer, I thank you. And if we could now move to the next page which is 2080. One of the things that you have discussed with us is the major -- major news media, sources. I think we need to go up a little bit more.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Madam Bolton.

utterances.text: Please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Now had you had mentioned in your testimony television press, and you had not mentioned the written press, I don't believe. Perhaps I'm mistaken, maybe you did. But with regard to --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I did --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: A with regard to the written press -- let me get there. With regard to the written press, would it be fair to say that during your tenure as an ambassador for Bosnia-Herzegovina, you read and considered information from those newspapers and news agencies that are listed on this particular schedule, including, and I want read them all, the New York Times, the Los Angeles Times, the Washington Post, the Christian Science Monitor, Reuters.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The list that I see at least goes down to Washington Post, as far as I can see.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let's, if we could, Mr. Registrar, scroll down.

But I'm going to spend some time with this particular document and this particular witness.

utterances.text: You're very correct, Mr. Guy-Smith. But, you see, you're putting the cart before the horse. utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I certainly don't want to ... I certainly don't mean to offend and didn't in any fashion.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could counsel please speak closer to the microphone.

utterances.text: In a fashion feel that it would foreclose --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure. I did not believe that that would foreclose an examination of information that's contained concerning -- within this document concerning issues which are relate and germane not only to challenging the Prosecution's case but also to developing the Defence case. But now, I stand -- I understand what the Court has said, and I also believe that there are two separate areas in which I find solace in my position. One is that under guidelines we have, and if you feel I have been, shall we say, a bit too quick in my position, that I can ask for you to reconsider. And the second area is under the fundamental rights that my client has under Article 21 to be able to, through cross-examination, not only, as I said before, challenge the case presented by the Prosecution but also develop a Defence. And, to be perfectly honest with you, I make a comment here, which is I find the view that the gentleman, at this time, is able to act as a mouthpiece for resolutions without being challenged, both in terms of his credibility in this regard by such information as is contained within this relatively comprehensive senate report, about something that I think is relatively critical to a number of issues, is troublesome. But in any event -- he is back. So at this point what I will do is I would ask, with the Court's indulgence, for it to reconsider its ruling, after a series of questions have been asked and answers have been given, whatever they may be, or ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You know --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm referring to the guidelines, I believe it's -- it's -- Rule 33. Your guideline, Rule 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mm-hm. I guess you do accept and understand, Mr. Guy-Smith, that, as a matter of procedure, and I'm sure this happens also in your jurisdiction, when a ruling has been made, it has been made. And on an issue like this where you are trying to admit a document, if the Chamber rules that it is not admitted, surely, you can't ask questions further on that document. I understand that there is a slight -- well, it is not slight. In my book it is a very fundamental difference, and it's a difference with which I have very great difficulty in this Tribunal, where documents are read, put on record, and after they have been put on record, only then they are sought to be admitted into evidence. They are already there. The procedure, as I know it, is that you authenticate and identify and authenticate and establish the nexus even before you ask questions about it, then you ask for admission. If it is it admitted, then only then can you ask questions. And if it is not admitted, that's the end of it, and that's the end of the life of that document. I hear you where you say you ask for reconsideration. We can reconsider. Let's hear what the Prosecution has to say. Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: My main concern again relates to the -- well, there's no -- there's no reason been proffered for reconsideration.
