One of the aspects of the discussion was the desire of the United Nations Security Council and many of the member states to have the area, if it could, devoid of all weaponry, because if there were no weapons, there could be no armed conflict; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. The problem was if weapons coming in as well as weapons that were already there, particularly in the hands of the JNA. But that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand that. And with regard to the issue of weapons coming into the region, and specifically weapons coming in to Bosnia-Herzegovina in violation of the embargo, those discussions concerned various parties. And I'm going to define parties in a minute. Correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: As long as you define parties, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. One of the parties that was of concern was a party that we spoke about before which was Iran. And I'm not asking at this point in any fashion whatsoever any -- any involvement you may have had or may not have had with regard to this issue, only the issue of the discussion being had.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: The context of discussion was not so much about the source as it was the entry. I believe you referred to some documents that again were post-war but during the United Nations, there wasn't this emphasise on the source, as there was and, in fact, the weapons that were coming in or were already there.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the issue of the weapons coming in, irrespective of the source of those weapons, a topic of conversation was the fact that those weapons were coming in, and the presence of those weapons in the region defeated the purpose of, among others, United Nations Resolution 713; correct?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct. Except I think you have added interpretation on the last part that I'm not sure I would agree with.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And when you say I have added an interpretation, if you could be so kind as to explain where you differ with my statement.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Which is the notion that it defeated the intention of Resolution 713. In fact the intention of that Resolution 713, as I think you so aptly pointed out before, was in fact to starve the whole region of all weapons, including the ones that were potentially coming in and including the ones that were already employed primarily by one side in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, the discussion of the weapons that were already in is as, I think, more appropriately discussion under, I believe, it is United Nations Resolution 752. And I think we will be having that discussion. But with regard to the issue of 713, and now I want to ask you whether or not you personally were aware of any information with regards to weapons coming into the region in violation of the United Nations arms embargo on January 22nd -- I saw your hand go up, Mr. Guirguis, and I'm more than happy to respect that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Okay, well, I'm go to -- I have to consult with the witness on this question. But you can finish your question, if you like. I didn't realize you weren't finished. But I'm going to object.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please finish, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: January 22nd, 1994.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Guirguis, I defer to you now at this time.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Regarding that, should we be muting, so that we don't hear their conversations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Madam, can you mute?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Could I perhaps have the question read back. I guess I don't understand the difference between this question and the topic area that had previously been raised and I understood the Court to exclude. I think he is asking about personal knowledge with respect to these matters, which the Court has already addressed. But if I'm incorrect, perhaps it would be clarified by having the question back.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, are you going to repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question is: With regard to the issue of 713, whether or not you were personally aware of any information with regard to weapons coming into the region, in violation of the United Nations arms embargo on January 22nd, 1994. And this is -- the issue is an issue of knowledge, not an issue of any personal involvement therein.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: Well, I'm sure counsel is aware that knowledge is something that can be charged under various forms, laws, and so I'm not particularly comfortable with that representation --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUIRGUIS
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... But in any event, Your Honour, I understand it's not my objection to make.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guirguis, please can we stick to what we are here for. You are here to advise your client, not to speak on his behalf. Advise your client what to say, and -- in response to this question and on his rights, and then let him say what he has to say. Your objection has no validity.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I think that -- I believe that the issue that gives me a little bit of pause is the language "personal knowledge," which, of course, I'm aware of numerous such information that I may have obtained through diplomatic or other channels.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, [Overlapping speakers]... Can I interrupt you, please. Can I interrupt you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yeah.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: We're not asking you to answer to the question. I'm asking you to tell whether you wish to answer the question or not to answer the question. Your counsel raised a hand because he wanted to give you advice on how who handle the situation.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Right. Now, can you tell us what you want to do, sir? Do you want to answer the question or not answer the question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I could answer this one question, but, I, of course, I wish to reserve my right to object to whatever follow-up may come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Madam Bolton is on her feet. Let's hear what she has got to say before I come back to you. Yes, Madam Bolton.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Sorry, the issue, I think, is that, previously, my friend had been asking question about the arrival of any specific shipments, did he have knowledge of that, and that was, I thought, an issue that had already been ruled on as not relevant. But I'm only going by my notes and not the transcript. So I stand to be corrected. Again, my issue is with relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, okay. I don't want even try to remember. I think I remember what -- I have a certain recollection of what was being discussed at the time, but I don't know want to say it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe at the time of the discussion was concerning self-incrimination and not relevance.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I thought -- but, actually, now that you say it, that discussion revolved around whether or not Mr. Sacirbey was involved in the ordering and procuring of arms from Iran from other countries to go for Bosnia-Herzegovina, not the question of whether he has knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I think, Your Honour, you're correct, and I apologise. I -- you have indicated the distinction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And I think that also clears Mr. Guirguis in New York. You said you can answer -- you will answer this question, and you still reserve your right on subsequent questions. Go ahead, Mr. Sacirbey.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do not recall any specific knowledge of the event that has been addressed here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm going to try to do this in a fashion where it is not quite as tedious. And what I'm going to do for the moment is read you a number of dates. Then I am going to stop, because your counsel may or may not wish to talk with you, or you may wish to speak with your counsel. If that is acceptable to you, sir, as a method for me to ask the following question, because I don't want to trap you in anything hear, okay?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that will be okay, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. I pose the same question to you with regard to the dates of February 7th, March 16th, April 4th, April 27th, April 30th, May 3rd, May 5th, and May 14th, 1994.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. -- we recognise the hand of Mr. Guirguis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no specific knowledge of these dates as in the context of what Mr. Guy-Smith has, I think, brought up. So I believe that's the proper answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The next dates would be May 19th and May 21st, and I stop there. If that causes any concern. Or I can continue.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I think the point was that I -- none of these dates would be of significance to me. First of all, because I really don't have the firsthand knowledge that you seem to be asking about. And, second of all, I'm not exactly sure of what the dates represent, when weapons may have been received, sent, some transit point. Clearly these issues are not within my personal knowledge. Or at least not that I would recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. If I understand your answer correctly, if I was to ask you the same question with regard to the dates of June 11th, 15th, 19th, July 23rd, August 17th, September 3rd, September 13th, September 20th, September 27th, November 3rd, and November 15th of 1994, I take it that I would obtain the same response with regard to you having no knowledge of when --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me make sure that I'm clear for the Court's record here.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me finish.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is, that I was part -- I'm sorry, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That you had no knowledge of when weapons may have been received, sent, some transit point as it related to the discussion at the United Nations concerning the lifting of the embargo. And specifically, the lifting of the embargo for Bosnia-Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I'm going to take issue with that question, Mr. Guy-Smith. It has absolutely nothing to do with this list. The discussions in the United Nations have nothing to do with this list.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: They may well. They very well may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: They may. It is it not apparent from the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, if you go back and take a look at the United Nations resolutions dates, and you take a look at the times of the minutes that have been received into evidence, and you make a comparison --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- of those, Your Honour. If I may finish my submission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Tell me, you interrupt me when I'm talking, and then you want to insist to finish when I can't finish my question, my point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I'm certainly not meaning to be -- [Overlapping speakers] ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... listen to me. The purpose of your questions is to seek admission of this document into evidence. And you're trying to establish a relationship between this witness and this document, not a relationship between the witness and what is taking place in the United Nations. For starters, this document talks about articles appearing in the National Intelligence Daily which you have established with a witness that is a CIA agent and not a United Nations agent. So that question about the United Nations has absolutely nothing to do with the witness's nexus with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Of course, it does.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: He may have information that he has from the United Nations, but you're trying to establish a nexus with this.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Of course, it does. It Absolutely does. If he receives information from the milk man and that information is germane to his position as a United Nations ambassador Bosnia-Herzegovina with regard to the issue of his desire to have the embargo lifted, it is it relevant, and there is a nexus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And it's relevant to establish a link with this document. Is that it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: It is certainly relevant information. And it may or may not establish a link for this document, and you may or may not rule with me with regard to the document, but with regard to the information that's contained therein --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You have --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- with regard --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the information that is contained therein, and the underlying issue that is of importance, it is relevant. And I believe there is a nexus.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Now you have asked this witness extensively about his knowledge about arms embargoes from his position in the United Nations. There was no problem with that. I am saying to you, I don't see any relevance to establishing a nexus between this witness and this document by asking him questions about the United Nations. That's what I'm saying to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I understand. Let me --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But any way, go ahead and do -- ask your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Let me see if I can -- if can I perhaps give you an idea of what my thinking is, because it may be of some assistance in terms of this particular aspect of this particular examination. We have heard evidence that there is a television set outside in the hallways of the United Nations and people saw that television set, and they saw a variety of publications with regard to that television set, and that information impacted or had the potential of impacting with regard to what the Prosecution has said is notice. So there is, obviously, apart from the fact that it is on the premises of the United Nations, there is obviously information which is being received by this witness which is information which impacted with this witness with regard to his job as a United Nations ambassador. Now, I'm asking him about another area where there is information which he may be aware of; he may not be aware. If he is not aware of it, so be it, then he is not aware of it. But if he is aware of it, because he has told us he received some information with which he learned at a later point, not directly, but indirectly came from the CIA, he learned he does not know whether or not he directly talked with people from the CIA, but he does know at some point in time he received information from the CIA. Here is another area where there is information from the central intelligence agency which he may have received. He may not have. That I don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If he has not, then he will tell us so, as he thus far, and we can move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But do you know, Mr. Guy-Smith. He has told you now that he has no recollection of these dates and what they are talking about. He has told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And to me, that's the end of the inquiry. But to begin to go beyond this document to other sources of information and want to use that to establish a link between the witness and this document, I find that irregular. Because you are rehashing subjects on which you have already cross-examined. And if you want to cross-examine this witness about what he knows in his capacity as ambassador, you don't need this document to do so. You can ask him those questions, and you have, indeed, done so without this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If I might, Your Honour, this -- this ties into the following question and answer that was made during the direct examination of Mr. Sacirbey at page 7141, beginning at line 7. "What sources of information did the Security Council have available to it, in terms of what was actually happening in the region?" Question. "A. First of all, they may have had various reports from the secretariat that is, United Nations representative agencies, whether it was UNPROFOR or such other missions or rapporteurs, as those who were institutions directly associated with United Nations, and there were multiple such institutions. They may have also received reports from other international institutions, for example, the EU monitoring mission. They may have received reports from related institutions, for example, various groupings of states and, of course, they would receive information from member states themselves and those member states might in fact also include media reports." It is our respectful submission that with regard to Mr. Sacirbey's answer and specifically starting at line 16, for example, various groupings of states, and, of course, they would receive information from member states themselves, that those member states would of necessity include information based on other answers that Mr. Sacirbey has given that come from intelligence agencies such as the CIA. And it in this that regard that I believe that the questioning of Mr. Sacirbey with regard to this issue is appropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: With respect, I don't agree with you, Mr. Guy-Smith. Based on that very answer that you have quoted. First of all, he is not saying they did receive. He say they may have. Right through that the paragraph, he says, they may, they may, they may. It is all speculative answer. And when he talks about media reports, could be any media reports. It is it very general. It may not necessarily be this media; it may be any other media report. We don't know. But what this witness has told us this afternoon is that he has no personal knowledge of these documents listed here specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take what Your Honour has said, and I'm reminded of guideline number 39, which deals with the issue of circumstantial evidence, and trust that the ruling and analysis just made by Your Honour concerning the qualified usage of language, and specifically the word "may," will apply to an analysis of this witness's testimony. If such is the case and the qualified use of that language, "may," by this witness will be viewed in the such a fashion so that an inference cannot be drawn, then I am comfortable.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have one more thing to say with regard -- because I think it might be of --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Carry on, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And I do apologise, Mr. Sacirbey, I don't know whether or not I received an answer for the balance of 1994 or not.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I think you did. You did, and that's when you went into his knowledge emanating from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As I'm looking at the record, unfortunately, I did not, Your Honour. Perhaps I'm mistaken, so I'd like if we could just have a quick view of the record to make sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah, you'll do that. Let me see if I can help you. Your last question on the document was: "I take it, therefore, with respect to the balance of the dates, your answer is going to be the same." And he said, Yes. Then you moved on to his knowledge from the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If you could be of assistance, if you could give me -- and I do apologise, Your Honour. I just need a page and line so I know where I am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Oh, I see.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Via videolink] Microphone, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I was saying, I'm not able to give him a page line because I was talking from recollection. And if I have to find the page, I have got to search like he was searching, you know. I'm doing it for the record.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Give me a second then, please, I do apologise. I see that my last question with regard to this particular issue is on page 71, line 6. And then without going into the question itself, at line 19, you interject, Your Honour, and I never got an answer to my question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Because your question starting at line 15 left your question from line 6 to 11, and now went to -- which was related to the dates, and now you were going to the United Nations, to his knowledge based on United Nations, and that's when I intervened. So if you want him to answer the question from line 6 to 11, if can you complete that, he can answer that.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you with us, Mr. Sacirbey?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I am, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, do you have a view of the screen with you? Are you able to read?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Are you referring to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The transcript.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were able to read when it was posted. I was able to read it when I was posted, but I have not seen anything for quite sometime now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. Then have you to have the question put to you again.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The question I asked you was: If I was to ask you the same question with regard to the dates of June 11th, 15th, 19th, July 23rd, August 17th, September 3rd, September 13th, September 20th, September 27th, November 3rd, and November 15th of 1994, I take it that I would obtain the same response with regard to you having no knowledge of when such violations occurred.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, you're largely correct. Subsequent to Dayton, the US initiative was called a train and equip programme to help rebuild the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina, pursuant to --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers]... I do apologise to you, Mr. Sacirbey, but you unfortunately are skipping away from the issue at hand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: And, Mr. Guy-Smith, I'm not quite sure -- you say now at page 79, I take it that I would obtain the same response with regard to you having no knowledge of when such violations occurred. I wonder whether that is the question. Whether the question is you would have no knowledge of these dates. The question that you were -- you have been asking about the dates, not the violations.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: The dates of these documents that are on the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I will be happy to reframe the question along the lines that His Honour has proposed in correcting the position that I have taken, and clearly rightfully so.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That you would have no knowledge of these dates as being dates in which violations occurred concerning the embargo.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Apparently, I didn't ask the question properly. And I'm not meaning -- I'm really not meaning not to ask the question properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: That's fine. I find myself in a situation where I'm doing what I shouldn't be doing. I shouldn't be asking you -- telling you how to ask your questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't want to you do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: But the point is, the point that you have been building up on is the witness's knowledge of articles that appeared on these dates that relates to violations that come from the national intelligence. Now he has said -- the question, as I understand it, should be, I take it, therefore, you say to me, you have no knowledge of any articles that appeared on these specific dates that I have given you, relating to violations of the embargo. That's what you are dealing with. You're dealing with this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Perhaps it's the difference between standing and sitting, Your Honour, but I think your question is an excellent question, and with your permission --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Would you like to sit down?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With your permission -- I would love to sit down. But with your permission, if I could adopt --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Mr. Guy-Smith, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If, with your permission, I could adopt your question, I think that would forward the situation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I would appreciate it if you would --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you mindful of His Honour's question?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I must say that I would like to have it rephrased. I'm just not quite sure I'm getting it. Thank you, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Surely.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I can hand it now, judge, but I appreciate any help I can get, you know. I'm a humble man; I will take help when I can get it.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I take it, therefore, you have no knowledge of any articles that appeared on these specific dates that I have given you, relating to violations of the embargo.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Any articles in what publications, Mr. Guy-Smith? The publications that you just noted?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have no -- that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Since you have answered by qualifying your answer, are you aware of any publications --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What do you qualify? I'm sorry. "I have no -- that's correct."

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Qualified by saying, Any articles in what publications? The publications that you just noted?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: So since you have qualified your answer with regard to, specifically, the publication noted, that being the National Intelligence Daily, I would ask you the same question with regard to any other publications.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Am I aware of any other publications that address the issue of arms embargo?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Violations.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Is that the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Arms embargo violations.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- I again would emphasise that the word "violations" is one that you have been utilizing, but, of course, I am aware of articles on this point.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: When you say the word "violation" is one that have I been utilizing, I take it that you were of a different opinion with regard to the introduction of weapons into the area as being a violation of --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: -- Resolution 713.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think -- I think, as you remember, Mr. Guy-Smith, and I think that His Honour asked me a specific question on this point. And that was did, in fact I, as representative of Bosnia-Herzegovina, consider the introduction of defensive weapons by the government of the republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina? After the aggression had started and after the genocide had started, did I consider that a violation of Resolution 713? I think my answer was very specific, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Are you aware of any publications with your definition in mind, apart from the National Intelligence Daily that discussed the issue of introduction of weapons into the area, which, in your view, was not in violation of 713?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard -- first of all, generally to those publications, are those publications that were the -- were the subject matter of United Nations Security Council discussions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are we speaking of official, informal discussions among ambassadors?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Sacirbey, you have pretty much told us throughout your testimony that there were both official and informal. If you would like I could start, of course, with the informal. Were there informal discussions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And did those informal discussions occur throughout the calendar year of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that that's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And the dates that have been mentioned to you and thus far, with regard to any publications outside of the Central Intelligence Agency publication, were those publications the subject matter of those discussions?

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: I am sorry, I don't know what my friend is referring to when he's asking about the dates mentioned to thus far. Are you talking about the other appendix we were looking at or...

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: No, I'm just referring to the -- I'm just referring to the dates in 1994 that I had mentioned before, starting in January 22nd and concluding with November 15th.

utterances.speaker: MS. BOLTON
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, I don't have any specific recollection to that -- to any of those specific dates. I have only recollections to general discussions regarding the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the general discussions regarding the matter, could you please amplify for the benefit of the Chamber how many of those discussions you had if you could.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was quite numerous. Probably at least ranging at -- certainly more than ten, probably less than 20.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Are you able to focus on any of those discussions occurring at or near the time of the passage of any resolutions during the calendar year of 1994?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: With great specificity, probably not.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. With general specificity [Microphone not activated] abstract of the other day, Your Honour. Let me rephrase.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yes, please. That cannot be general; that's a contradiction in terms.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what one would call an oxymoron. I'm in total agreement, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to general discussion, can you tie any of those to any specific resolutions?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Keeping in mind that there was always a reference to previous resolutions using subsequent resolutions on the subject matter, at least in general terms, perhaps. I think is the best answer I can give you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the discussions, can you help us at all here in terms of what the nature of the conversation was? And by that I mean in light of the fact that 713 was an active issue, one that is, as you've pointed out, was repeatedly mentioned and discussed in subsequent resolutions? Can you help us here as to what the nature of these conversations was? And by that I mean --

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. The -- most of the --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely. Most of the discussions were about the issue, whether in fact this was a violation of Resolution 713 and whether or not in fact there was any consistency, a conflict if you would, between various resolutions and as well as various principles of the right of self-defence and the needed to defend the population and the country. So clearly that was a constant topic.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: And with regard to the constant topic that you've mentioned, I take it obviously that the issue of Article 7 -- I'm sorry, chapter 7 became of some import?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you're speaking, of course, sometimes we speak of the Security Council, sometimes we speak of the United Nations. As you will recall, in the General Assembly starting December of 1992, there was a resolution of the General Assembly that specifically recommended that in fact the Security Council should, in fact, make it clear that Bosnia-Herzegovina was not bound by Security Council Resolution 713.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was something that was not adopted by the Security Council, however, was it.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was not. But it was an adopted by the General Assembly and we constantly had that conflict back and forth.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: As -- I take it, then, your position is that the passage by the General Assembly of position distinct from that of Security Council allowed for the different interpretation with regard to 713?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Actually, not. I think what 713 was -- what the General Assembly was suggesting is that the Security Council, in fact, should explicitly exclude Bosnia and Herzegovina. Bosnia and Herzegovina was never mentioned in the context of 713, since at that time it did not exist. The Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina did not exist as a member of the United Nations when it was adopted.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Overlapping speakers] ... only spoke of Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I appreciate that and that was part of the discussion that we had yesterday and part of this discussion you had with His Honour, and I'm not going to re-plow that particular field at this time. I take it that this same position, and once again now I'm talking about is your knowledge of the articles, would exist for the calendar year 1995; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Which articles?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The articles that are listed -- the articles that are listed in Appendix E of the document that we've been referring to, which is the final report of the select subcommittee to investigate the United States' role in Iranian arms transfers to Croatia and Bosnia ("the Iranian green light subcommittee"). And I'm referring to the following dates in 1995: Those being February 25th, May, 5th, June 2nd, June 10th, June 23rd, what I believe to be with my aged eyes is July 20 -- I can't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I am with you. I'm with you on that. I don't know whether the witness is.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: July ... July 24th, July 31st, August 11th, September 1st, October 3rd, November, what I believe to be the 17th, but I'm guessing, to be honest with you. December 11th, and December 28th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith, sorry, is there a question?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: We're going back to that old -- the old question that we dealt with some time ago, which is you're not aware of any articles that are in the national intelligence daily that dealt with the issue of violation of the arms embargo for those dates?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: In the year 1995 this time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I -- I believe the question that I originally understood was am I aware of the dates regarding any such, quote/unquote, violations, and the answer is no.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. And are you aware of any articles discussing violations on those dates?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: If we could have Appendix F on the screen, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What appendix is then that we already have?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That was Appendix E.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay. And what -- before we go to Appendix F, remember all these questions were being asked to establish a nexus between this witness and Appendix E, and Appendix we had -- you had asked that we reconsider. And all of this exercise was so that we [indiscernible] --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Based on the answers given by the witness at this time, I will be not moving its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You are?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I am not moving its admission based on the answers given by the witness at this time since the witness has indicated that he has no knowledge of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now, Appendix F, is that 1D03-2080?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Mair says that it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What does Mr. Guy-Smith say.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Mr. Guy-Smith follows the lead of Mr. Mair in this regard.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. You see there in front of you in Appendix F a series of articles and a series of dates. What I would like to do now is go through the pages that follow and go to 2081.

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's kind of a mess, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah. It's impossible to read except for the headlines, Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay. Well, we'll start just, if we can, perhaps with the headline.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're going to start this? How long are you going to take.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Well, I don't think it's going to take two minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: With regard to the first article on the screen, is this an article that you recall reading? And I'm asking that question by virtue of looking at the headline that is contained therein for the moment, because I don't think that you're going be able to see the writing as it is right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: You're going have give us an ID number of this document because now we are seeing this for the first time. This is not --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: This is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: This is not 2080.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: That's what it seems to ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: What is the ID number, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have it as 2080 on my screen right now. I'm double-checking.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I have it on my screen as 2081. The screen is reading it as something different from what it is. It's 2081.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Do you recall reading such an article?

utterances.speaker: MUHAMED SACIRBEY [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, Mr. Guy-Smith -- I'm sorry, Your Honour, did you interrupt?

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: He did -- [overlapping speakers]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: Yeah. But you go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: My -- first of all, I can't tell the publication nor the date; although, obviously the subject matter is familiar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Turning to the next one which is -- do you have a minute or not? Time?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
utterances.text: I will. I was saying we've passed the time. I'm sorry. Sorry, it's time to take a break at this time and once again, Mr. Sacirbey, the usual ritual: You don't discuss the case with anybody, not even with counsel next to you, until you are excused from testifying. We stand adjourned to tomorrow once again in the afternoon at quarter past 2.00, in Courtroom I for those who are here, and where you are there in New York. Court adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MOLOTO
